results.title: AI Is Fueling A Flood Of Customer Complaints. Is That A Bad Thing?
results.content:
So how should businesses respond to this flood of AI-generated complaints? And how can consumers make sure their genuine grievances don’t get lost in a sea of AI slop?

## Why Is There A Flood Of AI Complaints, And What’s The Problem?

It’s easy to see why people turn to AI when they have a complaint.

Many of us struggle with the dreaded blank page. We know something has gone wrong, but putting our frustration into words, explaining what happened and making a convincing case can be surprisingly difficult.

With a simple prompt and a few personal details, ChatGPT or Claude can produce a polished complaint letter in seconds, clearly outlining the problem and explaining why we’re unhappy. [...] And that neatly captures the dilemma. AI is making complaints more accessible, but it’s also making them harder to process.

## Should You Use AI To Write Complaints?

Absolutely. In principle, there’s nothing wrong with using AI to help write a complaint.

Getting our thoughts down clearly can be difficult, particularly when we’re angry, frustrated or unsure about our rights. AI can help organize our arguments, explain what went wrong and communicate what we want the company to do about it.

There’s even some evidence that AI-assisted complaints can lead to better outcomes.

But there are a few important things to remember. [...] And importantly, this means people who might previously have given up can now make their voices heard.

Think about it. In the past, how many people simply accepted poor service, unfair treatment or a disappointing product because complaining seemed like more trouble than it was worth? AI removes much of that friction, potentially bringing legitimate problems to light that businesses might otherwise never hear about.

But there’s a catch.

## AI doesn’t always know when to stop talking.

A review of the impact of AI-generated complaints across 11 countries found that submissions had increased in length in 76 of the 84 cases studied.

Many contained unnecessary details, irrelevant arguments and, in some cases, abusive or threatening language.

results.title: ‘Everyone's got a free lawyer': AI is making it easier than ever to submit complaints — but UK public bodies are struggling to deal with ‘AI clog’ | TechRadar
results.content:
In the pre-AI era, submitting a complaint took time and required research and a level of expertise. This level of effort acted as a natural filter to spurious complaints. But the release of AI chatbots such as ChatGPT to the general public has made it almost effortless to draft and submit a complaint to almost anyone.

But on the other end, human complaints handlers have to sift through a growing number of AI generated complaints with the same regard they would have for a human complaint, filtering out AI slop to get to the bottom of an issue.

In many cases, the complaints are “very long, repetitive and contain unrelated comments or misdirected demands,” Evans explained. “You get some huge ones. The worst one I’m aware of at the moment is about 200 pages long.” [...] # ‘Everyone's got a free lawyer': AI is making it easier than ever to submit complaints — but UK public bodies are struggling to deal with ‘AI clog’

Court backlogs and complaint resolutions are being slowed by AI

- Councils, authorities and caseworkers are struggling to filter through AI generated complaints
- AI makes complaining easier and that is contributing to backlogs in responses and the court system
- Workers are facing growing workloads without any extra budget

UK public bodies are struggling to deal with a veritable deluge of complaints that have exploded in both number and length with many public servants placing the blame squarely on the popularity of AI chatbots. [...] Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.

With the UK still facing a significant backlog on court cases, businesses battling legal complaints are having to spend significant amounts of money on cases brought against them by former employees using AI.

One business founder who is facing such a challenge said, “Everyone’s got a free lawyer now,” referring to how AI chatbots are making it easier to draft legal documents on behalf of plaintiffs.

Companies and authorities are contemplating a range of ways to deal with a growing backlog of AI generated complaints. Some are looking at enacting word limits on complaint forms to cut down on repetitive AI generated complaints, or moving complaints to a template form rather than a simple text box.

results.title: Managing the rise of AI-generated complaints and claims | TLT LLP
results.content:
## The balance to be considered

It would be wrong to treat every AI-assisted complaint or claim as a nuisance. AI can help consumers organise their complaints, overcome language barriers and make clearer arguments, which may particularly benefit some vulnerable and neurodivergent consumers. A well-structured complaint that identifies the real issue is easier to resolve, not harder. [...] # Managing the rise of AI-generated complaints and claims

Historically, it took time and effort for a litigant to raise a complaint or bring a claim and, in many cases, litigants relied on claimant firms for support. This has changed and the age of AI-drafted complaints and claims is upon us. Whilst the use of AI can help improve access to justice, it can also cause unnecessary costs and operational burden for those on the receiving end of the complaints and claims. AI may reduce the time and cost involved in producing a complaint or claim, but it does not necessarily reduce the time and cost involved in responding to one. In this update we consider this difficult balance and the need for careful management moving forward.

## The pressure on parties and the Courts [...] One risk for consumers is being persuaded into believing that a weak complaint is strong, rejecting a fair offer and pressing on to a hearing they were always likely to lose. A longer response does not necessarily contain more substance and every AI-invented rule still has to be checked before it can be corrected.

results.title: Consumer complaints to FTC on AI tools: Deceptive practices, poor service, sexual content | FedScoop
results.content:
The database provides a broad picture of the kinds of issues consumers can encounter with artificial intelligence chatbots. It includes accusations of throttled capacity and absent customer support agents. Some complaints outline more haunting experiences with AI, while others complain about crypto services they’ve confused for the Elon Musk-led firm xAI.

Here are unedited excerpts of a few of the complaints. The rest are available in full form here. [...] # Consumer complaints to FTC on AI tools: Deceptive practices, poor service, sexual content

A Federal Trade Commission database meant to guide law enforcement investigations now includes about 200 complaints against major artificial intelligence companies including xAI, OpenAI, and Anthropic, according to documents obtained through a public records request.

Those complaints include allegations of deceptive business practices and shoddy customer service, but also more severe accusations, including claims that these AI systems have joked about sexually assaulting children and spewed antisemitic rhetoric. [...] FedScoop isn’t able to verify the complaints, and it’s possible that these problems weren’t truly caused by the company, or that the allegations are unfounded. Still, the database provides a view into the varied kinds of frustrations people have with AI that are then brought to government investigators.

Anthropic and OpenAI declined to comment. xAI did not respond to a request for comment.

results.title: AI-Generated Complaints, Requests Flood Government Offices. It's Not Going Well | PCMag
results.content:
Public bodies in the UK are struggling to handle an influx of AI-written complaints and correspondence, which are often long and full of hallucinations, The Guardian reports.

AI chatbots may be useful tools for quickly whipping up an email based on a few bullet points or a single sentence, but when someone else has to read through it to find the point of the email, it can slow them down, especially if it references non-existent sources. That's the problem facing many public bodies, including lawyers' offices, local councils, schools, and politicians, who say they're struggling to respond to everyone, let alone effectively take action on their behalf.

“Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” Hollie Wickens, a senior case worker in a Labour MP's office, tells The Guardian. [...] Many of these submissions are legitimate; complaints about social care services, missed garbage collections, and potholes have surged. Those problems existed before AI, but the tech has made it easier to spin up a message and find the right person to send it to. It's also leading to a rise in appeals, as people can quickly put together a counterargument to a fine or warning. That said, lawyers told The Guardian that people often cite cases that don't exist or laws that apply in other countries or jurisdictions.
